title: Find your pulse: a minute with your own heartbeat
description: Two fingers, one quiet minute, and a number that tells a real story about your body. How to take your pulse properly — and what it can and cannot tell you.

body.heading: Finding it
paragraphs: Rest for a few minutes first. Place the tips of your index and middle fingers — not your thumb, which has a pulse of its own — on the inside of your other wrist, just below the base of the thumb, and press gently until you feel the beat.
Count the beats for thirty seconds and double the number, or count a full minute for the most reliable reading. That number is your pulse in beats per minute.

body.heading: What the number means
paragraphs: For most adults at rest, a pulse between about 60 and 100 beats per minute is considered typical, and people who are very fit often rest lower, because a stronger heart moves more blood with each beat. Your pulse rises with exercise, heat, illness, excitement and caffeine, and settles again as you recover.

A pulse reading is information, not a diagnosis. A single unusual number on an ordinary day is rarely a story; a pattern that worries you, or a racing, pounding or irregular beat with dizziness or chest pain, deserves a doctor promptly — and chest pain deserves urgent help.

body.heading: A small experiment
paragraphs: Take your pulse sitting quietly. Then walk briskly for two minutes and take it again. Sit down, and check every few minutes until it returns to your resting number.
You have just watched your cardiovascular system do its job: deliver more when asked, then settle. It does this thousands of times a day without being asked to.

takeaway: Two fingers and thirty seconds give you your pulse — a resting rate around 60–100 beats a minute is typical for adults, and patterns matter more than single readings.
